extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, public administrators, political scientists, and reformers interested in designing governmental intelligence/information systems
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating governmental or industrial 'intelligence' or information bureaux that collect, standardize, and present facts to decision-makers while preserving independence and preventing bureaucratic capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert role: prepare facts for decision-makers (not post-facto)
rubrics_metrics.description: The expert should first find and formulate the facts for the man of action, and later make what wisdom he can out of comparison between the decision, which he understands, and the facts, which he organized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the academic 'ex post facto' relationship in which social scientists merely rationalize decisions after the fact. The expert should stand in front of decision, not behind it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality: experts must not have a 'policy' or take sides
rubrics_metrics.description: The very last thing a decision-maker should tolerate is the suspicion that experts have a 'policy'—experts ought not to be reporters who advocate a line but should translate, simplify, and generalize without caring what decision is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experts begin to care too much about outcomes they 'see what they wish to see' and cease to represent the unseen environment faithfully. Maintain the expert as mirror and measure, not as partisan actor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of investigation and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The staff which executes should be separated as absolutely as possible from the staff which investigates; the two should be parallel but quite distinct bodies of men, recruited differently, paid if possible from separate funds, responsible to different heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This institutional separation is the chief safeguard against experts absorbing decision functions and becoming a bureaucracy. Design lines of authority, staffing, and incentives to preserve distinct roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial independence: secure funding beyond annual doles
rubrics_metrics.description: No agency of research can be really free if it depends upon annual doles from what may be a jealous or parsimonious legislature; the financial arrangement should insure the staff against left-handed attacks and provide for growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include a federal charter creating a trust fund, a sliding scale linked to departmental appropriations, and making the appropriation put beyond accidental interference so that abolition would require open repeal rather than covert strangling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure security for investigative staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure should be for life, with provision for retirement on a liberal pension, sabbatical years for advanced study and training, and dismissal only after a trial by professional colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the conditions of any non-profit intellectual career so staff have dignity, security, and the freedom of mind needed when they are not immediately concerned with practical decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access rights: legal entitlement to information and inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The bureau should have the right to examine all papers, to question any official or any outsider, and to propose accounting methods to the department; if proposals are rejected or violated, the bureau should be able to appeal under its charter to the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These access rights should be established in the organic act to prevent the staff from becoming subordinate to those who control information or files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional independence from departmental and congressional control
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence officials should be independent both of the Congressional committees dealing with that department and of the Secretary at the head of it; they should not be entangled either in decision or in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence turns mainly on funds, tenure, and access. If a Congress or official can deprive them of money, dismiss them, or close the files, the staff will become its creature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable standards and measures across bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: Various staffs should adopt, wherever possible, standards of measurement that are comparable and should exchange their records so that like things use the same measures and can be treated as competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition is useful only to the extent that the standards used to measure it are sound. Work to invent and refine index numbers (broadly defined) or other devices for comparative measurement of social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop quantitative indices to measure social qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The more you can analyze administration and work out elements that can be compared, the more you can invent quantitative measures (index numbers) for the qualities you wish to promote and turn competition to ideal ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index numbers need not be purely technical in the narrow sense; examples include comparative school-system indices and quota mechanisms used in public campaigns. Better indices make competition useful for social goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central clearing house / interdepartmental exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: A central clearing house should assemble facts in forms suited to particular problems and feed them to departmental intelligence bureaux; this central agency would become a focus of extraordinary information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a clearing house avoids duplication, makes information available in suitable form, and can serve the diplomatic, military, and economic needs of departments without ad hoc telephone memos and messengers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with universities for training and research
rubrics_metrics.description: The materials and staff of a central agency could be open to scholars; the central agency could become the makings of a national university with staff recruited from college graduates and work done in consultation with university curators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide steady turnover of temporary and specialist appointments from universities, exchanges of lecturers, and involve students in research to build training and recruiting together with the research mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional coordination via federations of bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of intelligence work applies equally to states, cities, and counties; federations of state/city/county bureaus can coordinate information so that regional combinations reconcile autonomy of decision with cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate accounting and information so administrative units can compare common problems (e.g., health, transportation) on a shared factual basis without necessarily centralizing decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target outputs to decision-makers; do not overload citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The intelligence bureau is primarily an instrument of the man of action—the representative charged with decision, and the worker at his work; its primary use is as an aid to representative government and administration, not to burden every citizen with expert opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some material will be useful for scholars and the press as a check, design outputs principally to help officials make decisions; voluntary societies and the press will mediate for ordinary citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make administration visible to encourage accountability and reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce agencies that will hold up a mirror week by week or month by month so officials and outsiders see the same facts; analysed and recorded work compared across bureaus moves argument to another plane beyond mere opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visibility reduces obstruction, diminishes pointless committee inquiries, and enables outsiders to judge both results and procedures; comparison with other bureaus or private corporations strengthens reform claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against bureaucratic dry rot through circulation and criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A network of intelligence bureaus might become a dead weight, but circulation of men, circulation of data, and circulation of criticism between government, industry, offices, and universities reduces the risk of red tape, pedantry, and ossification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design mechanisms for staff rotation, openness to external scholars, sharing of data, and critical review to prevent mountains of paperwork, redundant forms, and the growth of soft jobs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit secrecy: open material to scholars except necessary secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to see why all material, except a few diplomatic and military secrets, should not be open to the scholars of the country; this openness would feed real research and supply practical theses for students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance legitimate confidentiality with broad scholarly access to create a reservoir of trained analysts and to energize political science research tied to real governmental problems.
